review:
Fun momentum platformer.

It has a nice aesthetic, calming music and tight controls.
The narrative is nearly non existant, but serviceable.

I'd say one of it's biggest disadvantages is that it's pretty short. Sure, you have time attacks and collectables, but still.

In any case, I recommend this game, though I'd say it's better to grab it at discount.

Pensa numa experiência confortável no seu fim de tarde. Você pensou em Defunct!

Defunct é um jogo onde você controla esse robozinho simpático, que por acidente acaba caindo da sua nave mãe, e agora precisa percorrer diversos cenários e reestabelecer sua energia para retornar à nave. A história acaba ai, o jogo não conta com diálogos, mas o robô protagonista claramente possui uma personalidade que é transmitida pelas cutscenes e animações, como quando o robô acelera e ele fica batendo no próprio motor pra tentar pegar mais impulso, ele é uma graça!

O que dizer dos aspectos visuais desse jogo. Os modelos 3D seguem essa tendência que havia bastante na época do lançamento, de modelos mais simples com texturas mais cartoonizadas, e que funciona muito bem, ainda que bem simplório. E sim, você não está louco, toda a direção de arte e estética desse jogo lembram bastante Wall-E, nesse mundo onde a natureza tomou o lugar de tudo, e somente robôs existem.

O trabalho de som do jogo também é um ponto positivo. As músicas são bem legais e servem perfeitamente ao seu propósito, definindo o tom de cada momento do jogo, mas mais uma vez, nada que se sobressaia. No entanto os efeitos sonoros são um acerto em cheio.

A maior qualidade do jogo vem na sua gameplay, bem diferente do jogo de plataforma 3D tradicional. Aqui, você muda o ângulo do robô e acelera, podendo pular, se agarrar em paredes e usar um dash (está mais para um turbo do que necessariamente um dash), tudo isso baseado em momento, ou seja, mais íngreme o morro, MAIS RÁPIDO VOCÊ FICA! Sério, correr pelos cenários a 1000km/h é uma sensação tão satisfatória, e o jogo ainda que linear, conta com cenários bem amplos em espaço e verticalidade, então é possível fazer umas manobras bem interessantes.

"Se esse jogo é tudo isso, por que 3 estrelas somente?" Bem, é porque o jogo acaba ai mesmo. O tempo médio para o zeramento é de uma hora somente, e ainda que existam jogos curtos que são muito mais focados em narrativa e na experiência, como Portal, Sayonara Wild Hearts ou Superliminal, esse é excessivamente curto. Faltou tempo para eu me habituar bem com os comandos, e com toda a complexidade que a gameplay traz na movimentação, com somente esse tempo, sinto que estou jogando uma beta ao invés de um jogo inteiro propriamente dito. Quando eu menos esperava, os créditos estavam subindo. Parece que toda essa mecânica bem feita da movimentação foi muito mal usada, tendo em vista todas as possibilidades.

O jogo tem uma lógica Collectathon de pegar coletáveis entre os mapas para desbloquear uns extras para o personagem e manobras, mas o jogo não é construído de forma que te incentive a ficar andando lentamente em cada cenário para pegá-los, mas sim aproveitar o primeiro declive e correr mais do que o Sonic, então isso não adiciona tempo de gameplay prazeroso para o jogador.

No fim, é um jogo divertido. Peguem e joguem quando estiverem entediados, e saiam conhecendo um jogo muito bom, mas com um possível potencial descartado.

Defunct is one of those small little indie games with a cool and unique idea. You are a unicycle robot whose engine broke down inside a spaceship. You need to get to a repair shop. You need to use gravity to your advantage. You have the ability to gravitize to the ground. Doing this while going downhill will create momentum. On the way to the repair shop, you get launched outside of the spaceship onto the planet's surface. You now have to find a way back to the spaceship. You traverse different areas of the planet and solve small puzzles. You sometimes enter a big area with buttons scattered around. You have to find a way to activate them all to open a gate. The feeling of speed is addicting and you're always on the lookout for the next big slope to gain more momentum. This gameplay belongs in a Sonic game. It's a short little experience with a bit of replay value thanks to time trials, collectibles and alternate routes.

Um jogo de exploração 3D bem relaxante, onde o jogador controla um robô monociclo. Nesse jogo, é possível pegar velocidade rapidamente nas descidas ao pressionar o gatilho RT, mas com a desvantagem de ocorrer desaceleração rápida se o gatilho continuar sendo pressionado nas subidas. 

Acelerar até o final das rampas faz o robô pular mais alto. Quanto maior a velocidade, mais alto e longe o robô irá. Além disso, é possível aderir às paredes e aos tetos ao segurar o botão Y. Essas técnicas são importantes para coletar muitos dos itens colecionáveis opcionais.

A maioria das fases são focadas em progredir com velocidade, coletando os itens de turbo e as poções de velocidade. Algumas fases possuem alguns puzzles envolvendo ativar alguns interruptores vermelhos, mas nada complexo demais.

O jogo é curto, os checkpoints são abundantes, e as vidas extras infinitas. Uma ótima jogatina para servir de pano de fundo enquanto se ouve algum podcast.

The entire story takes about an hour and a half to complete if you do no size content (puzzles and collectables). It's a cute little story with little depth about a damaged robot falling from home & racing to get back with the help of a few PlanetSide dwellers. It's a near silent experience but reminiscent of 2000's mascot games like Ratchet & Clank, Jak or Tak in aesthetics.

[H3]Controller Support[/h3]
If you plan to play on controller, a few menus require keyboard & mouse input to access including the unlockables menu in level select. During gameplay your gamepads buttons won't be displayed in tutorial tooltips instead opting for keyboard & mouse, leading to an inconvenient learning experience.

[H3]Gameplay[/H3]
The gameplay is momentum based. You'll need to find a balance and connect with some awkward controls in conjunction with the inclines & declines to gain & maintain speed and control throughout the levels. Momentum can be lost swiftly if you aren't utilising the weight shifting controls near perfectly which could cause frustration during certain levels as you forage for a decline to regain speed.

[H3]Replayability [/H3]
There is replayability here if you're one to challenge yourself for better times or others via the level select screen & time trial mode; further evident by the various speed runs uploaded on the internet, a featured run at Games Done Quick in 2016 and steam discussions, whether the community remains is unknown but you can challenge yourself.

There's also the unlockables menu where you can change your robots colours & view tricks, both earned by gathering collectables during each level, collectables that are either hidden in secret areas or require agility to obtain.

[H3]Conclusion[/H3]
Despite enjoying the world & aesthetics of Defunct, the gameplay was not for me which is why I chose to not recommend the title as it's very short and the controls are troublesome.

[B]While I had issues with the controls & content I believe those who enjoy testing themselves, improving on time trials & competing with others could find themselves enjoying Defunct given they can enjoy the momentum controls. To those people I recommend picking it up during sales for $1.12AUD.[\b]

Defunct, developed by Freshly Squeezed and published by SOEDESCO, is a vibrant and fast-paced indie adventure that centers around one simple but captivating concept—momentum. The game places players in control of a small service robot that has accidentally fallen from a massive cargo ship and now must race across the surface of a deserted, post-human Earth to return before being left behind. This premise serves as both narrative backdrop and gameplay metaphor; everything in Defunct is built around the idea of motion, speed, and the joy of fluid traversal. Rather than relying on combat or complex objectives, the experience is shaped entirely by how gracefully you can move through the environment. It’s a game about mastering gravity, reading terrain, and finding that perfect flow state where every jump and slope feels effortless.

The world of Defunct is a futuristic yet strangely serene wasteland where humanity has long vanished, leaving behind remnants of their machines and technology. What might sound like a bleak setting is instead one of quiet beauty. The landscapes are wide, colorful, and full of rolling hills, deserts, and metallic structures, all designed to be traversed rather than fought over. You guide your little robot across these environments using a combination of speed-boosting mechanics and gravity manipulation. The robot’s “Gravitize” ability allows it to alter its personal gravity field: activating it downhill accelerates your speed, while using it uphill slows you down. This creates a rhythm of play that rewards smart terrain reading and timing—momentum becomes both your weapon and your challenge. The learning curve is gentle at first, but as the game progresses, mastering when and how to engage Gravitize becomes the key to maintaining velocity and chaining together exhilarating runs.

From the very beginning, Defunct makes it clear that it values feel over flash. The controls are tight and responsive, and the sense of speed, once you find your rhythm, can be intoxicating. Sliding down slopes and launching into the air before chaining into another hill feels remarkably satisfying. The inclusion of magnetic surfaces that allow you to cling to walls or ceilings adds another dimension to movement, and creative players can use these moments to string together daring shortcuts or recover from missed jumps. When everything clicks, Defunct delivers a sense of flow that few indie games manage to achieve. It captures the same kind of momentum-driven thrill found in classics like Sonic the Hedgehog or modern parkour-inspired titles, but with a personality all its own. The best moments occur when the level design and physics merge perfectly, creating stretches of terrain that feel like natural roller coasters—fast, smooth, and endlessly replayable.

Visually, Defunct uses a stylized, almost painterly aesthetic that complements its focus on movement and exploration. The world feels open and organic, with environmental storytelling hinted at through abandoned machines, rusted cities, and scattered remnants of civilization. The design doesn’t rely on excessive realism but instead uses color, light, and shape to evoke atmosphere. Each region has a distinct palette that reinforces its identity—lush valleys, sunburned canyons, and mechanical ruins all flow seamlessly into one another, giving a sense of journey even though the game is relatively short. The soundtrack is equally well-crafted, with ambient electronic music that shifts smoothly between energetic and reflective tones, depending on the pacing of each stage. Combined with the mechanical hum of your robot and the whoosh of air as you race downhill, the sound design creates an immersive sense of motion that enhances every moment of gameplay.

Yet for all its strengths, Defunct is not without flaws. Its biggest limitation is its length; the main campaign can be completed in just a couple of hours, leaving players wishing there was more to explore. While the game does include time trial challenges and optional collectibles to extend playtime, the core experience feels more like a sprint than a marathon. Once you’ve mastered the physics and learned the optimal routes, the replay value becomes largely dependent on your desire to chase better times rather than discover new content. Some segments also break the game’s pacing by introducing slow or puzzle-oriented sections that contrast sharply with the otherwise high-speed design. These moments, while brief, disrupt the flow and remind you that Defunct is at its best when it lets players move freely rather than forcing them to stop and solve minor obstacles.

The technical performance is solid for such a small-scale production. The game runs smoothly, loads quickly, and maintains stable framerates even at high speeds, which is crucial for preserving the sensation of fluidity. The physics engine, while occasionally imperfect, generally holds up well, though players might occasionally encounter awkward collisions or moments where the camera struggles to keep up with fast movement. These are minor blemishes on an otherwise well-optimized experience. The developers have clearly prioritized smooth gameplay and control precision over visual extravagance, and it pays off—Defunct feels polished where it matters most. The UI and menu design are minimal, keeping the focus on momentum and exploration rather than distraction.

Defunct’s narrative is minimal but thematically fitting. The little robot’s journey to return home doesn’t need dialogue or exposition to resonate; its struggle speaks through action. There’s a quiet melancholy in racing through a world that once belonged to humans but is now inhabited only by machines and the echoes of a vanished civilization. The environmental storytelling hints at a deeper history without spelling it out, leaving room for players to interpret meaning at their own pace. It’s a world that feels lonely yet peaceful, fast yet reflective—a paradox that gives the game emotional depth despite its brevity. The absence of overt storytelling reinforces the idea that motion itself is the story. Every hill conquered and every boost executed perfectly becomes a small act of triumph in an otherwise desolate world.

In the end, Defunct stands as a reminder that games don’t need to be massive or complex to be memorable. It’s a love letter to movement—a kinetic experience that values the physical sensation of play above all else. The combination of its fluid controls, vivid environments, and expressive world design creates a game that is both calming and exhilarating, meditative and fast-paced. Its short runtime and occasional pacing hiccups may prevent it from reaching greatness, but within its limited scope, it achieves something rare: pure, unfiltered motion that feels alive. Defunct is best approached as a compact, joyful ride rather than a sprawling adventure—a few hours of momentum and grace that linger long after the credits roll.

Es un juego corto que acabé en 53 minutos. Me gusta mucho que el personaje sea como una motocicleta, lo cual es el punto de comparación más sencillo. Me parece bastante suave y relajador de manejar y aclaro que, aunque podría categorizar este juego como un runner plataformero, se toma la libertad de ser más un runner que ser un plataformero.

No existen enemigos, solo eres tú y un mapa con el suficiente espacio como para que no choques mucho y puedas aprovechar los boosts y colinas para aumentar tu velocidad. Me encanta que, el juego sabe tan bien que te gusta ir lo más veloz posible, que añade una sección en la que haces literalmente una carrera. JAJ.

Me encanta, creo que aprovecha demasiado bien el mapa y el movimiento del personaje y me pareció una experiencia bastante satisfactoria. No me arrepiento de haberlo probado, pero sí de darme cuenta de lo corto que es.

La única pega para mí (la cual buscaré de desahogar pero no crean que es algo importante que arruina la experiencia, sino más bien un berrinche de mi parte) es que, si bien no intenta contar una historia profunda (y está bien), sí añade cinemáticas que me da que no aportan muchísimo a la experiencia como las veces que el protagonista le sucede algo como caerse o chocarse o cuando, como respuesta a esto, añaden una cinemática del mismo levantándose y/o posicionándose para que luego juegues.

Me hubiese gustado que fuese así como un Half Life, cuyas  "cinemáticas" no detienen al jugador. 

Pero da igual, ya que en total todas las cinemáticas dan alrededor de 6 minutos en total y creo que estoy siendo generoso. El juego me pareció excelente.

[h1]Reseña del Juego: Defunct - Un Viaje a Toda Velocidad en el Cuerpo de un Robot Despistado[/h1]

[h2]Resumen[/h2]
Bienvenidos, fanáticos del vertiginoso mundo de los videojuegos, donde Defunct te pone en los zapatos... bueno, en las ruedas de un pequeñín robot que parece que tomó demasiadas dobladas a la derecha, perdiendo al resto de su flota. Si alguna vez soñaste con ser un R2-D2 con un turbo incorporado, este podría ser tu chance de brillar... o de patinar, dependiendo de tu habilidad.

[h2]Aspectos importantes e interesantes[/h2]
Lo primero que salta a la vista es la velocidad a la que este robot, aparentemente ensamblado con partes de una aspiradora y un monopatín, puede alcanzar. La sensación de velocidad es palpable y logra ponerte ese nudo en la garganta cuando más lo aceleras. Acompañado con una mecánica de juego que involucra acelerar por pendientes para ganar velocidad y un uso peculiar de la gravedad, Defunct te tiene más tiempo en el aire que en el suelo, lo cual es divertido... hasta que te estrellas por enésima vez. Además, los paisajes son un festín visual de colores y formas, un verdadero arte abstracto a 100 km/h.

[h2]Aspectos por mejorar[/h2]
Los controles pueden llegar a ser tan rebeldes como un adolescente evitando hacer su tarea. Te encontrarás a menudo peleando con el teclado más que disfrutando del paisaje. Además, la historia es tan profunda como un charco en el desierto, lo cuales es una oportunidad desperdiciada. Y, sí, los diálogos y efectos sonoros tienden a la repetición que podría hacer que tu periquito empiece a repetirlos.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

Defunct is a momentum-based action platformer with an emphasis on building and maintaining speed.

It is a fun concept, but it is indeed a short game. While I personally would rather have a short, fun game than a long, tedious one, it is beatable in under an hour if you just play through the main adventure. I think the game really opens up when you go through the levels in Time Trial mode. For that reason, I think you will enjoy this game more if you treat it more like a racing game with defined tracks and times to beat rather than a straight platformer.

Pros:
- Movement is fun and intuitive, with a great sense of speed once you get the hang of it.
- Time trial mode has realistic yet difficult times to beat.
- The robot designs are cute, with the main character being expressive and appealing

Cons:
- The main game is very short (<1 hour).
- The story and cutscenes are paper thin.

Oyuncular, yer çekimi motoru kullanarak farklı yer çekimi alanları oluşturabilir ve hızlarını artırarak dünyada gezinebilirler. Oyun dünyası, çeşitli hız destekleriyle dolu ve oyuncular garip robotlarla tanışarak, hurdalıklarda uçarak ve gemilerine geri dönmek için yolculuk ederler.

Görsel olarak, Defunct, güzel bir dünya sunuyor ve yer çekimi motoruyla yaptığınız hızlı hareketler oldukça keyifli bir deneyim sunuyor. Oyunun 11 seviyesi, farklı iklimler, biyomlar ve mücadelelerle dolu. Oyuncular, ana karakterin görünümlerini kilitleyebilir ve özel numaralarla herkese ders verebilirler. Ayrıca, oyuncular, fazladan 5 seviye içeren süre denemesi modunda en iyi tamamlama sürelerini elde etmek için mücadele edebilirler.

Defunct, hızlı ve etkileşimli oynanışı ile dikkat çeken keyifli bir macera oyunudur. Oyunun grafikleri, oynanışı ve özellikleri ile ilgilenen oyuncuların ilgisini çekebilir.
